<https://ro.co/perspectives/super-bowl-economics/|Ro's Super Bowl: >A few of you have sent me the Ro Super Bowl breakdown and I loved it. Here are some more thoughts and context from my experience:
• *$146 million:* To understand Ro's situation, they spent $146 million reportedly in paid media in 2025 per Media Radar. Certain channels like digital tend to be underreported in these systems, but let's assume it's in the $150-$200 million range. That means their paid media Super Bowl commitment (not including production or teaser / surrounding campaigns, and assuming their budget doesn't rise drastically this year) is about 7-13% of their media budget.
• *Short term results not guaranteed:* I appreciate the piece's note on this that while short-term Super Bowl results are entirely possible, even the best case is often solid, but perhaps not spectacular. Let's take <https://adage.com/video/coinbase-qr-code-1m57s/|Coinbase> for example, one of the better performing SB ads of the last few years. The ad reportedly drove 20 million site visits, which was apparently 18% of Super Bowl viewers that year - that's massive. But sign-ups were 445k - a 2% conversion rate on site visitors. Very solid, but still a drop off, and these sign-ups don't necessarily represent customers. And that's one of the best case scenarios. In my experience, I've seen similar results; either great traffic with immediate drop-off, or an ability to beat the category for the next 7 days, but not at sky high levels. Ultimately, the Super Bowl should be the start or part of a long-term marathon, not a one and done short-term sprint (and if you run in it, get those retargeting pools ready).
• *Awareness going in:* There are a lot of factors that go into a successful SB spot - creative, placement (I swear, I once saw a report that said the best time to run your spot is before 9:27PM), quality of the game, pod position, etc. But an underrated one is existing brand awareness. <https://www.linkedin.com/posts/danny-weisman-33b45045_the-most-loved-ads-of-super-bowl-lvii-t-mobile-activity-7032349637353078784-hBfc/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAD-PAz4BXF9HuiUKCy8RgRej2tdRixrcxhI|I wrote a post a few years ago about Farmer's Dog,> and while their ad was universally beloved and had the highest viewership of any ad that year given their placement pre-halftime show, their lack of awareness leading into the game might have stunted some of their momentum coming out of it. Check it out, and it's something to think about - the Super Bowl might be tough to make an unknown brand truly known, vs. be the first domino to fall for a growing brand to explode.

Measurement around the Super Bowl ads has been amazing.

And it's pointed out something interesting with The Farmer's Dog.

If you're not familiar, The Farmer's Dog won the Super Bowl. No, literally - they won USA Today's Ad Meter.

Per SambaTV, they also had the most reach of any Super Bowl ad, reaching 27.6 million households - 4.4 million more households than the lowest reaching Super Bowl ad from E*TRADE.

That's because their ad aired strategically right before halftime, as people started tuning in awaiting Rihanna. So Farmer's Dog was able to get a 16% cheaper CPM vs. E*TRADE, just for knowing the right spot to place their ad.

And yet...per Morning Consult (honestly, one of, if not the, best measurement companies out there right now IMO), did not have Farmer's Dog in their top 10 most loved Super Bowl ads.

Huh? The ad about the dog lasting your entire lifetime wasn't in the top 10 most loved? What gives?

That's because - as my contact at Morning Consult surmised:

"Could be linked to low brand awareness (I've been surprised by that in past Super Bowls).. Simply put, the impressions that an ad lands will only be recalled if they are made in association with the brand."

So despite reaching the most homes of any Super Bowl ad because of a savvy media placement, The Farmer's Dog's low awareness heading into the game may have stunted its momentum coming out of it.

Now, this is just one datapoint, and Farmer's Dog Google Trends seems to be still healthy post-Super Bowl.

But it's a lesson to brands thinking a Super Bowl ad will get their name on the map. If their brand name isn't already established, a Super Bowl ad may get attention, but not association. 

(Thanks to Maren Kirlin for the insights above!)

But sign-ups were 445k - a 2% conversion rate on site visitors. Very solid, but still a drop off, and these sign-ups don't necessarily represent customers. And that's one of the best case scenarios. Hi all I've invited everyone to a Rolls-Royce brainstorm this afternoon. Very much optional to attend. Here's the brief:

*Deck from client here:* <https://drive.google.com/file/d/1US9RQpN1fI-cI0GDle7t_oD5EJOMhIgc/view?usp=sharing>

*Brief Overview*
Rolls-Royce activation in Shoreditch where they'll be showcasing a graffitied car by artist Cyril Kongo, followed by a VIP club night.

They're keen for us to do something around the activation but they don't want it to be branded as a paid partnership (Rolls-Royce don't do ads). They have some budget (amount not disclosed but I'm thinking around £20k-£30k).

We need to put together a proposal for what we could do to cover the the reveal of Black Badge x Cyril Kongo in Shoreditch, as well as any ideas for how we could create buzz & excitement around this new car/collaboration

*Objectives of the overall showcase + any coverage*
Cars are already sold, so the story is really about raising awareness RR's bespoke capabilities, showcasing the art of the possible with RR - and how RR transcend automotive as a House of Luxury.

Aside from announcing the collaboration, coverage should reinforce RR's positioning as a House of Luxury, and positioning of Black Badge (the brand’s more subversive alter ego), as well as amplify our Bespoke message. Also authentically position us in the world of art.

*Our Approach*
We're pitching this as a Caliber Collective 'social partnerships' product, and would like to treat TNM as the hero publisher, but also incorporate other publishers, e.g. Capsule, and/or any other publishers in our orbit who we think would be a good fit such as art creators & publishers.

We could revolve the proposal around a central white label asset we create that gets amplified by different social publishers such as TNM, with each publisher modifying the asset to suit their style/audience (similarly to what we did with Movember Confession Box)… but open to other approaches.

*Other info*
Cyril will be available for interviews, can do a live graffiti showcase (in venue/outside venue). We’ll have a Deniz Menendez DJing in the space for both the media / VIP activity.

The cars are all built but the process has been filmed so we can incorporate that footage into our content.

*Who will be attending*
We’ll have art/lifestyle media attending in the afternoon, getting the deeper dive and exclusive opp to enrich their storytelling.
Evening is VIPs (our little black book of influential contacts from the worlds of art,music, culture etc) alongside RR clients

My team is attending two events 5,000 miles apart this week. 

Starting today, our founder & CEO, Ramin Beheshti, will be in Vail, Colorado for the Digiday Publishing Summit leading a panel on how Caliber has built a next-gen publisher that leans into creators, at a time when competition for attention has never been higher, and orgs are needing to compete with (or in our case, embrace) the creator economy. The panel will be on Wednesday 3/25 at 9:45am - it's can't miss. 

Even more, with AI creeping into every corner of our work, Ramin brings a unique, technological expertise to the table from his past work leading product & tech at Dow Jones - a great person to speak to on all things AI and future of publishing (or his Liverpool fandom), even outside of his creator-focused panel. 

Changing gears...on the other side of the Atlantic, we've got Will Hamnett and Scott B. bopping around Advertising Week Europe in London. They'll be at the event meeting with partners and friends, new and old, but you can also find them at **Daly's Wine Bar at 5pm** on Tuesday 2/24 for a hang and chat on the new landscape of media partnerships, sales and growth. Two guys I respect a ton, who have been around the block and have a lot to share. 

If you're in either of these places, drop me a line (or message them on LI directly) and we can get you set-up for a coffee, a pint, or just a chat.

The brands winning on social right now? They're not trying to reach everyone - they're trying to matter to someone.

The best social strategies I've seen didn't come from media buyers, they came from comms people; and the difference is where they start. Not with distribution, not with platform, not with budget. With narrative. Who actually needs to hear this and why would they care enough to do anything with it?

Reach is cheap now. Platforms will put anything in front of anyone if you throw enough money at it, which means reach stopped being the differentiator a while ago. Knowing your audience well enough to say something that actually lands with them - that's where the real work is.

It's why Caliber is built the way it is. We're not trying to be everywhere, we're trying to be the authoritative voice for specific communities who are genuinely paying attention.

Jake Schneider is at #SocialMediaWeek this week talking about exactly this - what a comms-first social strategy looks like when you actually put it into practice. Worth tracking him down if this is your world.

You don’t need 1B views. Getting there is like chasing the sun across a lawn that keeps getting shredded by John Deere-riding execs.

I mean, it's a great number that feels good. I should know: I’ve clocked that number at newsrooms and brands over the past 20 years. Find me one person on the content side of media who doesn’t love knowing their work is reaching eyeballs.

But as lovely as that reach is for our editorial egos, it’s not nearly as useful to a long-term content strategy that drives business.

I prefer another approach: Be everything to someone, not something to everyone. 

Users have been trained to expect algorithmically curated content experiences that speak directly to what they care about, from politics to pickleball. At Caliber, we’re hyper-conscious of this. Our brands — The Recount, The News Movement, The Caliber Collective, SaySo — are driven by the same belief: precision beats volume.

If this sounds like your kind of thinking and you're attending ADWEEK's Social Media Week, definitely reach out to Caliber's Jake Schneider — he'll be there to talk more about what we're building.

attachments.text:
As a fan of TBPN for a while, I have mixed feelings about the OpenAI acquisition.

When I saw their President, Dylan Abruscato, discussing TBPN's future a few months ago at the NYSE, the focus was on making the current show as good as it could possibly be - not new IP, not new talent, not building a multi-channel media company...I wonder if that will continue to be the strategy, and if they will be able to remain impartial and deliver the hot, smart takes their fans have grown to love. OpenAI is definitely a smart company, and Sam Altman is without a doubt a smart guy, so if he knows what he's buying (which I think he does), I don't expect the programming to change much, if at all. 

What really strikes me, though, is the acquisition being rumored to be in the low-mid 9 figures, for a less than 1 year old media company with around $10m in annual revenue. With Caliber being a high-growth media company ourselves, that's an exciting number to see, and it also underscores the importance of something we've been talking about for quite some time. 

Niche over reach. 

In casual conversations amongst friends, it always amazes me how many of them who aren't in tech or media have just never heard of TBPN. I feel like it's all I've been seeing the past 6 or so months. But it shows the power of a niche audience that focuses on being everything to someone, rather than something to everyone. They know who they're speaking to, they know what they care about, and the partners they bring into their ecosystem...actually make sense. 

Reach is easy...and these days, it's pretty cheap.

Building an audience that schedules their day around consuming your content -kind of like the early 2000's cable TV, linear as king days (I know, funny) - is a much taller task, and as we've just seen, delivers a much bigger payoff. Somehow TBPN was able to do it VERY quickly - that's not normal. 

I just rewatched 'There Will Be Blood' last night (and it was as good as I remembered), so I'll leave you with this analogy inspired by the opening scene.

The bigger the explosion, the longer the fuse. Take your time, listen to your most loyal followers, readers, viewers, etc...or it just might blow up in your face.

Why you don't want 1 billion views.

In case you weren't aware, it's ADWEEK's Social Media Week next week here in NYC. In a sea of conferences it's genuinely a good one…

However, over the weekend I saw it being marketed as an event where you could "meet the social media teams behind viral campaigns."

Yes, I'd like to meet these people - I’m sure they're lovely - but are we really still obsessing over viral campaigns and billions of views in 2026?

I got my start in social media almost 10 years ago at Jungle Creations, back when Facebook was the dominant platform and social feeds were chronological.

We were masters of producing viral branded content - so good at it in fact that we won a Lion at Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity - and I got to work with the world's biggest brands.

But scale was never the hard part. The hard part was and is proving that the right people saw it, and that it actually changed something.

We recently ran a campaign for Walmart's 'Open Call' - their annual program backing American manufacturers and small businesses. Creator-fronted, social-first content, built to reach U.S. policymakers and opinion shapers through The News Movement, creator channels, and Walmart's own channels.

The measurement was as precise as the distribution...working with Swayable (who we love), we tracked double-digit lifts among policymaker and opinion-former audiences on the exact reputation metrics Walmart cared about - perceptions of their support for small businesses and American manufacturing.

For us at Caliber, social in 2026 is about being everything to someone, rather than something to everyone...so I always wince when I hear that sort of line above. 

Conversations about niche over reach are what we want to be having at Social Media Week. Not how do we go viral, but how do we actually land with the people who matter to us?

If that's a conversation you'd like to be a part of, Jake Schneider and I will be there next week. Hit us up!

attachments.text:
You don’t need 1B views. Getting there is like chasing the sun across a lawn that keeps getting shredded by John Deere-riding execs.

I mean, it's a great number that feels good. I should know: I’ve clocked that number at newsrooms and brands over the past 20 years. Find me one person on the content side of media who doesn’t love knowing their work is reaching eyeballs.

But as lovely as that reach is for our editorial egos, it’s not nearly as useful to a long-term content strategy that drives business.

I prefer another approach: Be everything to someone, not something to everyone. 

Users have been trained to expect algorithmically curated content experiences that speak directly to what they care about, from politics to pickleball. At Caliber, we’re hyper-conscious of this. Our brands — The Recount, The News Movement, The Caliber Collective, SaySo — are driven by the same belief: precision beats volume.

If this sounds like your kind of thinking and you're attending ADWEEK's Social Media Week, definitely reach out to Caliber's Jake Schneider — he'll be there to talk more about what we're building.

attachments.text:
As a fan of TBPN for a while, I have mixed feelings about the OpenAI acquisition.

When I saw their President, Dylan Abruscato, discussing TBPN's future a few months ago at the NYSE, the focus was on making the current show as good as it could possibly be - not new IP, not new talent, not building a multi-channel media company...I wonder if that will continue to be the strategy, and if they will be able to remain impartial and deliver the hot, smart takes their fans have grown to love. OpenAI is definitely a smart company, and Sam Altman is without a doubt a smart guy, so if he knows what he's buying (which I think he does), I don't expect the programming to change much, if at all. 

What really strikes me, though, is the acquisition being rumored to be in the low-mid 9 figures, for a less than 1 year old media company with around $10m in annual revenue. With Caliber being a high-growth media company ourselves, that's an exciting number to see, and it also underscores the importance of something we've been talking about for quite some time. 

Niche over reach. 

In casual conversations amongst friends, it always amazes me how many of them who aren't in tech or media have just never heard of TBPN. I feel like it's all I've been seeing the past 6 or so months. But it shows the power of a niche audience that focuses on being everything to someone, rather than something to everyone. They know who they're speaking to, they know what they care about, and the partners they bring into their ecosystem...actually make sense. 

Reach is easy...and these days, it's pretty cheap.

Building an audience that schedules their day around consuming your content -kind of like the early 2000's cable TV, linear as king days (I know, funny) - is a much taller task, and as we've just seen, delivers a much bigger payoff. Somehow TBPN was able to do it VERY quickly - that's not normal. 

I just rewatched 'There Will Be Blood' last night (and it was as good as I remembered), so I'll leave you with this analogy inspired by the opening scene.

The bigger the explosion, the longer the fuse. Take your time, listen to your most loyal followers, readers, viewers, etc...or it just might blow up in your face.

attachments.text:
Why you don't want 1 billion views.

In case you weren't aware, it's ADWEEK's Social Media Week next week here in NYC. In a sea of conferences it's genuinely a good one…

However, over the weekend I saw it being marketed as an event where you could "meet the social media teams behind viral campaigns."

Yes, I'd like to meet these people - I’m sure they're lovely - but are we really still obsessing over viral campaigns and billions of views in 2026?

I got my start in social media almost 10 years ago at Jungle Creations, back when Facebook was the dominant platform and social feeds were chronological.

We were masters of producing viral branded content - so good at it in fact that we won a Lion at Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity - and I got to work with the world's biggest brands.

But scale was never the hard part. The hard part was and is proving that the right people saw it, and that it actually changed something.

We recently ran a campaign for Walmart's 'Open Call' - their annual program backing American manufacturers and small businesses. Creator-fronted, social-first content, built to reach U.S. policymakers and opinion shapers through The News Movement, creator channels, and Walmart's own channels.

The measurement was as precise as the distribution...working with Swayable (who we love), we tracked double-digit lifts among policymaker and opinion-former audiences on the exact reputation metrics Walmart cared about - perceptions of their support for small businesses and American manufacturing.

For us at Caliber, social in 2026 is about being everything to someone, rather than something to everyone...so I always wince when I hear that sort of line above. 

Conversations about niche over reach are what we want to be having at Social Media Week. Not how do we go viral, but how do we actually land with the people who matter to us?

If that's a conversation you'd like to be a part of, Jake Schneider and I will be there next week. Hit us up!

Hey all!

Wanted to share the GoPuff pitch from yesterday <https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1DrEfSulLXc-DRzotBcbdTpuNDp3S2CK-jLyVXpJtMV8/edit?usp=sharing|here>.

BIG shout outs to <@U0841SJRLFN> <@U06TRLR09CL> and <@U09104V5VR9>  for really bringing this to life! A lot went into this in a short space of time!! Thanks to everyone else who touched this project, gave feedback and supported.

Some of the feedback in the room from the client was really excellent, you could tell he left feeling excited, and thinking about all the possibilities of how we could work together. Part being that Jake had done a great job warming him up and building that relationship, and he was a client that truly understands social and knows there are things they need to do on their side to become a social first brand.

A challenge he mentioned was that their leaders are very social first, but not strategic - they see other brands going viral with something and immediately shift their focus and say “we should do this”

This is EXACTLY what we are writing about in the next version of drop - called (title tbc) “The Copy Cat Crisis” so it’s really interesting to see this is clearly an issue out there for brand managers, this could be something they can download and send to their bosses.

Something I wanted to add, at previous agencies I’ve been - a pitch deck and pitch process like this would have taken an 6 weeks or more, a full dedicated team of 12 working on it full time and half of them wouldn’t even have the TikTok app on their phone plus unnecessary hurdles to go through that block the creativity. In my opinion, we've matched the quality (and then some) with less faff, and FAST. It’s just to say that regardless of the outcome, it makes me excited that we are so agile and with such talented teams, we can turn around great ideas at speed - which makes it feels like the possibilities are endless!!

VICE NEWS AND ADOBE ACROBAT GIVE AUDIENCES A NEW WAY TO STEP INSIDE THE STORY REPORTING ON-THE-GROUND FROM THE BIGGEST WAR GAME IN AFRICAN HISTORY 

Our VICE News team is on the ground in Morocco, embedded with more than 5,600 troops and U.S. paratroopers conducting drills at Cap Draa at African Lion 2026, the largest annual military exercise on the African continent with more than 40 nations in attendance.

Shane Smith and the team are there to report on this year's defining showcase: AI-enabled command and control, warfare autonomous systems, counter-drone capabilities, and advanced surveillance and reconnaissance platforms. 

To make sense of the enormous volume of documents, data, and source material coming in from the U.S. Africa Command and our own team’s research in the field, VICE News has partnered with Adobe Acrobat and their new PDF Spaces capabilities. Using PDF Spaces in Acrobat, our team can synthesize and interrogate hundreds of pages of planning, scenario, and research documents on the fly – helping our reporters stay accurate, move fast, and make smart decisions about what to cover. When we publish a finished story for our audience, we can also share the documents, research and source materials with our audience, giving them the ability to explore the evidence, ask their own questions and engage with the story on a deeper level. This delivers exactly the radical type of transparency that audiences demand today. 

Speaking from Tan-Tan, Morocco, VICE Founder and VICE News Editor-In-Chief Shane Smith said: "Now more than ever, audiences need transparent, fact-based, nonpartisan journalism. And as we build VICE News for a new generation, we’re proud to partner with Adobe Acrobat and take our audience even further into the story.” 

Check out some of our reporting in the video below. 

The link to the VICE News African Lion PDF Spaces - the first of an ongoing series - is in the comments. Are you ready to step inside the story with us?

over 2 years ago, i posted that trends alone cannot build a brand on social. that thought has since evolved...

i was initially referencing trending sounds, memes, and everyone feeling like they needed a mascot on tiktok for some reason. now, we are in a fully fledged “YOU NEED TO DO” economy

"YOU NEED TO REACTIVE TRENDS"
“YOU NEED TO DO MINI DRAMA CONTENT”
“YOU NEED TO DO BRAIN ROT”
“YOU NEED TO DO EMPLOYEE GENERATED CONTENT”

it’s social content whiplash. 
WE’RE IN A COPYCAT CRISIS. 

in caliber's latest edition of the drop, we’re talking about how (and we've been talking about it for awhile) ORIGINALITY, PURPOSE and PLATFORM COMPREHENSION are key for building brands on social in 2026. 

p.s this isn’t some lofty deck with 100 slides of theory. social does have a science, but it can be simple.

full report here: <https://lnkd.in/e6NNW2Hp>
